policy_title: Raise Skilled Worker and Family Visa Income Thresholds with Inflation
stated: The Conservative Party will automatically raise the Skilled Worker visa salary threshold and the Family visa minimum income requirement with inflation to ensure they do not undercut UK workers.

source.quote: Going forward, we will raise the Skilled Worker threshold and Family income requirement with inflation automatically to make sure they don’t undercut UK workers.

bearing_set.reason: Maintaining real-terms salary floors on Skilled Worker visas directly affects whether employers can use immigration to undercut UK workers' wages and job security — a non-negligible labour-market verdict.

The Family visa minimum income requirement determines which UK residents can exercise the legally recognised right to family life (ECHR Art. 8) by sponsoring a non-UK spouse or partner; uprating it with inflation preserves a significant legal barrier to that right.

Inflation-indexed thresholds reduce the pool of affordable overseas talent for employers in genuine skills-shortage sectors; if firms cannot fill roles or face higher payroll costs to do so, aggregate productivity and business investment indicators are moved — a genuine contested tradeoff against the wage-protection benefit.

The family visa minimum income requirement raised with inflation raises the earnings bar for sponsoring family members, directly making reunion harder for lower/middle-earning sponsors; the mechanism (fewer family reunions → reduced belonging and community ties for affected households) maps directly onto O15's belonging and loneliness indicators.

membership_note: Three genuine bearings: O4 (wage protection mechanism), O13 (employer talent-access tradeoff), and O15 (family visa income bar restricts reunion, affecting belonging). Fiscal effects are negligible (no material O12 movement); O9 not triggered as the threshold applies on its face equally to all nationalities; O2 effects on consumer prices too indirect and diffuse to clear the non-negligible bar.
